title: NASA's CAPSTONE 02 Will Test Autonomous Docking and Formation Flying Around the Moon
summary:
Navigating the space around the Moon is notoriously difficult due to the combined gravitational pull of Earth and the Moon, creating what are called three-body orbits. To master this environment, NASA has announced CAPSTONE 02, a follow-up to the pioneering CAPSTONE mission. Targeted for launch in 2027, it will deploy two identical 400-kilogram spacecraft built by Terran Orbital Systems to practice rendezvous and proximity operations—essentially, how to find and safely approach another vehicle in cislunar space.

The original CAPSTONE, short for Cislunar Autonomous Positioning System Technology Operations and Navigation Experiment, was the first U.S. commercial lunar mission and the first to operate in a near rectilinear halo orbit. It validated key navigation and communication technologies. CAPSTONE 02 shifts from validation to active demonstration. The twin spacecraft will switch between chaser and target roles, testing autonomous navigation using optical sensors, ground tracking, and celestial references. This is far more complex than docking in low Earth orbit because the gravitational landscape is constantly shifting.

These capabilities are crucial for the Artemis program. When astronauts in an Orion capsule reach the Moon, they must dock with a lunar lander to descend to the surface. CAPSTONE 02 will test three NASA-developed navigation software suites during a low-energy transfer trajectory that swings past the Moon before settling into orbit. It will also carry an optical imaging payload from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory to capture lunar imagery. The mission further matures the Cislunar Autonomous Positioning System, which allows spacecraft to determine their position relative to each other without relying on Earth-based tracking.

“This mission represents an important step in the maturation of cislunar capabilities,” said Sean Fuller, Moon Base CAPSTONE manager. By demonstrating cost-effective, scalable mission models, CAPSTONE 02 lays the groundwork for future lunar infrastructure and commercial services supporting Artemis, Moon Base, and deep space exploration.
why_it_matters: Mastering autonomous docking around the Moon is a key puzzle piece for the next generation of lunar exploration and future missions to Mars — the careers you might one day join are being prototyped right now.

background_read: The space between Earth and the Moon, called cislunar space, is governed by the three-body problem — an area of physics where the gravity of two large bodies creates unpredictable orbital paths. The original CAPSTONE mission, launched in 2022, was the first U.S. commercial lunar mission and the first to fly in a near rectilinear halo orbit, a wobbly but fuel-efficient path near the Moon. The upcoming Artemis program aims to return astronauts to the lunar surface by the mid-2020s, requiring Orion capsules to dock with lunar landers far from the simpler low Earth orbit. Autonomous docking is essential because signals from Earth take over a second to reach the Moon, making remote piloting risky. Terran Orbital Systems, the company building the twin spacecraft, has experience with small satellite technology, while Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory provides advanced optical instruments for lunar surface imaging.

perspectives.description: Successful autonomous docking will make lunar landing missions safer and more reliable, helping astronauts reach the surface and return. It also opens the door for commercial companies to service future Moon bases, creating a new economy in space.

Focus on the Moon can divert funds from other needs, like Earth-observation or deep-space telescopes. The complexity of three-body orbits also introduces risk: if the software fails, spacecraft could be lost in the gravitational tangle.

Historically, docking in low Earth orbit was a Cold War-era achievement; doing the same near the Moon is an order of magnitude harder because the gravitational environment never stays constant. CAPSTONE’s approach of using small, low-cost satellites is part of a broader shift toward faster, cheaper space testing.

Once autonomous rendezvous is proven in cislunar space, the technology could be adapted for asteroid surveys, orbital fuel depots, and even Mars assembly missions. Future lunar stations may rely entirely on robotically docked supply ships, mimicking an interplanetary shipping lane.
